newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon refuses comment on pilot adultery trial.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon refuses comment on pilot adultery trial.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen refused Tuesday to comment about the court-martial of the nation's first female B-52 bomber pilot on adultery charges but said the military had high standards that had to be enforced.

"We have very high standards for the military," Cohen said in an interview with ABC's "Good Morning America." There are reasons for maintaining these high standards in order to have discipline and high morale."
Cohen declined to comment further about the case involving Air Force 1st Lt. Kelly Flinn, scheduled to go on trial at Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota Tuesday.
"It would be inappropriate and improper for me to comment in any way about this case," he told ABC.

But when asked if adultery should be an imprisonable offence for military personnel, Cohen said: "We expect them to function under extraordinary circumstances and so we do have different standards for those in the military than those in civilian life."
In an interview Tuesday with the Cable News Network, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman John Shalikashvili was asked if the U.S. military was targeting the crime of adultery.
"I have certainly no such indication," he said.
"My sense is that all the leaders I speak to try very, very hard to apply the uniform code of military justice fairly, speedily and evenly."
Flinn, 26 and single, acknowledged having an affair with a married civilian. She was also acccused of having sex with a lower-ranking enlisted man and of lying.
She sought to resign with an honourable discharge to avoid court-martial on charges of adultery and fraternisation.
But a senior air force official told Reuters on Monday it was unlikely Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall would grant Flinn, an honourable discharge to avoid court-martial on charges of adultery.
"It is going to be very, very unlikely that the secretary will allow an honourable discharge," the official told Reuters when asked if Flinn's request for the step would be granted.

Other air force officials said that the charges were much more serious than adultery, because they involved fraternisation with a lower-ranking air force enlisted man, as well as lying and disobeying an order.

First Lt. Kelly Flinn, who is 26 and single, is seeking to resign from the Air Force with an honourable discharge in order to avoid being court-martialed on charges including adultery and fraternisation.
She acknowledged having an affair with a married civilian and also having sex with a lower-ranking enlisted man, which are violations of the military code of conduct.
Unnamed Pentagon officials said on Monday Flinn was unlikely to receive an honourable discharge from Air Force Secretary Shiela Widnall.

LaMarca told reporters that officials at Minot Air Force Base asked the Pentagon whether to proceed with the trial after Flinn's lawyers submitted her resignation request Monday afternoon. LaMarca would not comment on how long it would take the military justice division to respond.
